internal_discovery.plain_explanation: Across the 42 packet occurrences the consonantal skeleton b-ḥ-r carries two Quran-internally unrelated meanings. In 41 occurrences (all singular/dual/plural of baḥr: baHr, baHrayn/baHrān, abḥur, biḥār) it denotes a large, bounded, countable body of water — the world's water-domain set in explicit opposition to barr (dry land): the medium ships run in (2:164, 22:65, 31:31, 17:66, 42:32, 55:24), habitat of fish and ornament (5:96, 16:14, 18:61, 18:63), a mass crossed/parted/dried/calmed (2:50, 7:138, 10:90, 20:77, 26:63, 44:24), and the referent of the ink-simile (18:109, 31:27). This water class is internally coherent and salinity-neutral (25:53, 35:12 call a sweet/fresh water baḥr). But one occurrence, baḥīra (5:103:5:1), sits in a closed list of fabricated consecrated-livestock categories (sāʾiba, waṣīla, ḥām) with no water, ship, barr, or fish content whatsoever. Its only tie to the sea class is the bare tri-consonantal root plus the ear-slitting etymology of external lexica — both barred by the source policy. With no Quran-internal bridge across these two senses, the honest root-level judgment is UNRESOLVED: the packet contains at least two homographic lexemes and cannot be unified into a single nucleus. internal_discovery.layer_separation_note: Within the water class the root does NOT entail: salinity (fresh ʿadhb furāt is a baḥr, 25:53:4:2, 35:12:3:2); navigability or ships (vessels are always separately lexicalized as fulk/jawārī, and a baḥr can be made a dry road, 20:77:12:2); danger/impassability (it is split 26:63, calmed 44:24, traversed 10:90); mere 'water' as substance (it is a bounded count noun that dualizes and pluralizes: baHrayn 18:60, abḥur 31:27, biḥār 81:6); and it is distinct from nahr/anhār, which are named as a separate category alongside it (14:32, 27:61).
